lines: The Extraordinary Voyages

Jules Verne · Around the World in Eighty Days, Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, A Journey to the Centre of the Earth, From the Earth to the Moon, Five Weeks in a Balloon, Robur the Conqueror, The Mysterious Island

Jules Verne keeps the book of his voyages in his house on the quay: Phileas Fogg's wager, Captain Nemo and the Nautilus, Professor Lidenbrock's descent, the Gun Club's shot at the Moon, Dr Fergusson's balloon, Robur's Albatross and the castaways of Lincoln Island. A tour of them all, a chapter from each, as he wrote it.

Verne opens the book
Around the World in Eighty Days
The quay of the Voyages, and the round-towered house at its corner
Go into Verne's house on the quay: the round-towered corner house.
Find Jules Verne at his desk in the Library of the Voyages.

'Ah, a reader! Sit, sit. I keep a card for every fact I ever read: twenty thousand cards, and every one of them is in a book now. Here is the one I am proudest of: The Extraordinary Voyages . Every voyage I ever wrote, from the Reform Club to the bottom of the sea, from Iceland to the Moon. You shall make them all, the way my people made them. Start where I would start: with an Englishman and his clock.'
The catalogue of the Voyages
Look through the catalogue of the Voyages: every book Verne wrote, in order.
Verne's notebook of facts
Verne's notebook is on his desk, by the fact cards. Pick it up: you will need it.
🃏 One of Verne's cards

'Here's one from my box. Mr Fogg says a man can now go round the world in eighty days. The Daily Telegraph worked it out: London to Suez, Bombay, Calcutta, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, New York, London. Which way round does he go?'
East, with the Sun coming to meet him
West, chasing the Sun
Over the North Pole
West would be the other way round: Fogg goes out through Suez and India, east.
No one went over the Pole in 1872, not even in my books... yet.
Out onto the quay. Verne's house door.
The Globe of the Voyages
Walk to the Globe of the Voyages on the quay and see where every voyage begins.
Walk along the quay to the Reform Club: Pall Mall, London, in Verne's harbour.
A card from Fogg's whist table
The Reform Club, Pall Mall, 2 October 1872
Andrew Stuart, engineer, member of the Reform Club, 1872: brusque, sceptical, sure Fogg's wager is madness. He bets four thousand pounds against him.
Eighty days! Including bad weather, shipwrecks, railway accidents? Absurd.
Gauthier Ralph, a director of the Bank of England, Reform Club, 1872: worried about the fifty-five thousand pounds stolen from the Bank that very week.
Have you heard? Fifty-five thousand pounds, taken from the Bank's own counter. The thief won't get far.
John Sullivan, banker, Reform Club, 1872: a calm man of figures who has the Daily Telegraph's estimate of the eighty days by heart.
The Daily Telegraph has it worked out to the day, you know.
Go into the Reform Club.
Listen to Gauthier Ralph at the whist table: the news of the bank robbery.

'Fifty-five thousand pounds, gentlemen, taken from the cashier's table of the Bank of England. A well-dressed gentleman, they say. The detectives are watching every port: Liverpool, Glasgow, Havre, Suez, Brindisi, New York. Where could he go?'
▶ 'The world is big enough'
Andrew Stuart thinks the thief will get away: the world is big enough.

'It was once,' says Mr Fogg quietly, not looking up from his cards. 'The world has grown smaller. A man can now go round it in eighty days.' Stuart lays down his cards. 'I would like to see you do it, in eighty days.' 'It depends on you. Shall we go?'
Hear Phileas Fogg make the wager at his table.
▶ 'Diamonds are trumps'
John Sullivan has the Daily Telegraph's figures. Ask him how the eighty days add up.
📰 The Daily Telegraph

London to Suez, by rail and steamboat: 7 days. Suez to Bombay, steamer: 13. Bombay to Calcutta, rail: 3. Calcutta to Hong Kong, steamer: 13. Hong Kong to Yokohama: 6. Yokohama to San Francisco: 22. San Francisco to New York, rail: 7. New York to London, steamer and rail: 9. Total: 80 days. 'All included,' says Mr Fogg, and plays on.
A card from the whist table
The hand is finished. Pick up a card from Fogg's whist table, for luck.
Look at the race board: who has made the voyage, and how fast.
Out onto Pall Mall. Passepartout is waiting with the carpet bag.
Passepartout and Mr Fix
Passepartout's carpet bag tag
Pall Mall, then the steamer quay at Suez

Mr Fix, a detective of Scotland Yard, 1872: thin, sharp-eyed, nervous, certain that Phileas Fogg is the Bank robber. He follows Fogg round the world waiting for a warrant, and tries to win Passepartout's trust over a drink.
Excuse me, sir... you wouldn't happen to be travelling with a Mr Fogg? An English gentleman, very exact? Just a friendly question.
The British consul at Suez
The ship chandler's
The British consul at Suez, 1872: a fair, unhurried official who signs passports and will not refuse a visa to an honest traveller just because a detective wants him delayed.
Passports? Of course. Every traveller's paper gets my stamp, if it's in order.
Talk with Passepartout outside the Reform Club. He has just been told they leave in ten minutes.

'Round the world! In eighty days! And I who wanted a quiet life! Monsieur has put twenty thousand pounds in banknotes in this carpet bag. "Take care of it," he says. Take care of it! I shall hold it like my own heart.' And in his hurry, he has left the gas burning in his room, at his own cost, all the way round.
▶ Off to Charing Cross
The Gare des Voyages
Walk to the station on the quay: the Dover train, a quarter before nine. (Then on by the steamer: Paris, Mont Cenis, Brindisi, Suez.)
Seven days later, the quay at Suez. A thin, nervous man is watching every passenger off the steamer Mongolia.

'I am Fix, of Scotland Yard. The robber, gentleman-like, is coming through Suez, I'd wager my place on it. If he's on the Mongolia, I'll know him. And here comes his servant, with a passport to be signed.' He studies Passepartout as a cat studies a mouse.
▶ 'Where is your master?'
Fix asks the consul to refuse the visa. Go with them to the consul.

'I can't refuse a visa to an honest man's passport,' says the consul. Fix bites his lip: there is no warrant yet. Mr Fogg arrives, has his passport stamped with perfect calm, and goes back on board. Fix sends a telegram to London: Have found the bank robber, Phileas Fogg. Send without delay warrant of arrest to Bombay.
Fix's telegram to London
Fix has dropped the copy of his telegram on the quay. Pick it up and read it.

Mr Fogg's notebook: Left London Wednesday, October 2nd, 8.45 p.m. Reached Suez Wednesday, October 9th, 11 a.m. Total hours: 158½; or, in days, six days and a half. Is he ahead of the Telegraph's plan, or behind?
Ahead: the plan allows 7 days to Suez
Behind: the plan allows 6 days to Suez
Look again at the Telegraph: London to Suez, 7 days.
Six and a half is not seven.
Passepartout is going ashore to buy shirts. Warn him about the friendly stranger.

'Monsieur Fix? A charming fellow! He showed me the canal and the town. He asks a great deal about Monsieur, it's true... Bah, everyone is curious about an Englishman who goes round the world for a bet.' The Mongolia's whistle blows: on to Aden and Bombay.
Watch the Mongolia steam out of the harbour towards the Red Sea, with Fix on board too.
A pocket watch set to London time
Round the world, and the day that was found

Aouda, a Parsee lady of Bombay, educated in England, rescued by Fogg and Passepartout in India from a forced death on a funeral pyre. Brave, gentle and clever, she travels round the world with them and in the end marries Phileas Fogg.
Mr Fogg saved my life in Bundelcund. I have seen him calm through storms, a typhoon and an attack on a train. I think he is the best man in the world.
Mr Fix, the detective, at the end of the voyage, ashamed: he arrested Fogg in Liverpool on the wrong man's description, and the real thief had been caught three days before.
I... I was wrong. Tell him I was wrong.
The voyage itself: go into the Reform Club and take Fogg's wager for yourself.
Phileas Fogg's table
Make the race round the world from Fogg's table: London, Suez, India, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, New York, home, in under eighty days.
Aouda is waiting in the Club. Ask her what happened in India.

'The railway stopped: the line was not finished. Mr Fogg bought an elephant, Kiouni, for two thousand pounds, and we crossed the forest. That night they found me: drugged, to be burned beside my dead husband's body on the pyre. Passepartout took the dead man's place under the shroud, rose up in the smoke, and carried me out before them all. They thought he was the dead raja come back. Then we ran.'
Mr Fix has something to say.

'I arrested him at Liverpool, with my warrant, on the 21st of December, at twenty minutes before twelve. The robber, Fogg? The real thief was taken at Edinburgh three days before. I let him go at half past two. He knocked me down; I deserved it. But the train to London had gone. He came in at ten minutes to nine. Five minutes too late.'
Sit with the lost wager a moment. Twenty thousand pounds, gone; everything Fogg had left, gone.
Next day: Passepartout runs out to the clergyman to arrange Fogg's wedding to Aouda. And comes running back.

'My master! Tomorrow... impossible! The wedding... Today is Saturday!' 'Saturday? Impossible!' 'Yes, yes! You have made a mistake of one day! We arrived twenty-four hours ahead of time; but there are only ten minutes left!' Fogg had gone east, toward the Sun, and so the days had been shorter by four minutes for each degree: three hundred and sixty degrees, twenty-four hours.
Going east round the world, each day is about four minutes shorter than at home. How much do the minutes add up to, all the way round?
Twenty-four hours: a whole day
Four minutes, three hundred and sixty times...
Every degree east, the Sun comes four minutes sooner.
Into the Reform Club's great saloon, as the clock strikes. 8.44... 8.45...
He is there. Speak to Mr Fogg.
⌚ A quarter before nine

'Here I am, gentlemen!' Fifty-seven seconds after twenty minutes past eight, he came through the door. Phileas Fogg had won his wager of twenty thousand pounds. He had spent nearly nineteen thousand on the way: he gained little but the journey. And Aouda, who became his wife.
▶ Close the chapter
The monster of the seas
Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea
A shell from Nemo's museum
1866: something enormous in the sea

Pierre Aronnax, professor at the Museum of Natural History in Paris, 1867: a careful naturalist, author of 'The Mysteries of the Great Submarine Grounds', who thinks the sea monster is a giant narwhal. He is invited aboard the frigate Abraham Lincoln to hunt it.
A narwhal of enormous size, I should say: sixty yards long, with a horn of steel. But we shall see.
Commander Farragut of the American frigate Abraham Lincoln, 1867: a good seaman who believes in the monster as he believes in God, and has sworn to rid the seas of it.
The Abraham Lincoln sails from Brooklyn tonight. Are you with us?
Go into the Geographical Society, where the papers are full of the monster.
Professor Aronnax has written an article about the monster. Ask him what it is.
🐋 A giant narwhal?

'In 1866 ships saw a long object, phosphorescent, far larger and faster than a whale. The Scotia was holed below the waterline: a triangular hole, clean as if cut by a tool. A hole in iron plates an inch and a half thick! Only a narwhal of extraordinary size, with a horn of steel, could do it. That is my view; I have published it.'
Commander Farragut invites the Professor aboard the Abraham Lincoln.

'Sir, if you will consent to join the Abraham Lincoln in this expedition, the Government of the United States will with pleasure see France represented in the enterprise.' Three seconds later the Professor said yes. 'Conseil!' he called, 'we leave in two hours.'
The examiners' desk
Before you go, the Society's examiners want to know you can find your way at sea.
Out of the Society.
Down at the Nautilus dock, the harpooner Ned Land. In the book he is the 'king of harpooners', and does not believe in narwhals.

'A narwhal? Bah. A whale, maybe. I've struck two hundred of them. But a fish that cuts through iron? I'll believe it when my harpoon finds it.' Three months later, off Japan, the thing was found. Ned's harpoon struck it and rang, as if against metal. Then a blow, and the Professor was in the sea.
Conseil, the Professor's faithful servant, jumped in after him. Hear how it ended.
🌊 On the back of the monster

'If master would be so good as to lean on my shoulder, master would swim much better.' They swam all night. At dawn they found Ned Land, sitting on the back of the monster. It was not an animal. It was made of iron plates, bolted together. And then the plates opened, and eight men in masks drew them inside.
A shell washed up on the jetty
A shell on the jetty by the iron hull. Pick it up.
Go aboard the Nautilus.
Aboard the Nautilus
Nemo's motto: Mobilis in Mobili
The Nautilus, all by electricity
Captain Nemo receives you in the great salon.
